title: Architecture contrast: long-context & routing hotspots
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a cross-model comparison (Llama-style dense, Mistral-style dense, and Qwen-style dense/large-context variants) focused on long-context performance and where MoE-style routing introduces hotspots in the serving runtime. The goal is practical: identify consistent bucketed bottlenecks across models and suggest targeted mitigations we can prototype in the runtime (scheduling changes, routing prefetch, kernel fusion points).

Environment & test harness:
- Hardware: p8d.24xlarge equivalence (A100 80GB), single-GPU microbench + multi-GPU aggregation runs. Also reprobed on A2/A10 for kernel variance.
- Runtime: internal serving-runtime v3.9.2 with continuous-batching enabled, kv-cache prefix-caching ON, default scheduler.
- Models and configs tested (representative checkpoints):
  - Dense-L: Llama-2-13B-like, seq_len slices 2k/4k/8k
  - Dense-M: Mistral-style 7B/8k long-context variant (chunked positional approach)
  - Dense-Q: Qwen-14B long-context (native rotary scaling + extended-kv)
  - MoE hybrid test: 8-expert gating layer inserted at mid-depth (synthetic expert params to simulate routing fanout)
- Workloads: streaming decode (top-p sampling), batched small requests (B=4..32), single large-context requests (single session, long prefix), and concurrent mixed workloads.
- Tracing: per-op NVTX, per-kernel timing, TPU-like kernel heatmaps (our heatmap exporter), and per-thread queue wait histograms.

Quick summary of high-level findings:
1) Attention memory growth dominates wall-clock for seq_len > 4k on dense models: not just compute FLOPs but frequent device-host gather/scatter for KV slices and attention index shuffles cause latency cliffs.
2) Mistral-style architectures with chunked attention show better sustained throughput at long context because they reduce attention compute but increase indexing and extra kernel launches — trading compute for kernel-launch overhead.
3) Qwen long-context shows relatively stable latency for prefix-heavy workloads due to rotary/kv layout optimizations, but experiences high memory fragmentation under heavy concurrent caching, leading to OOMs in mixed workloads.
4) MoE routing hotspots concentrate at: gating softmax, topk argpartition, and per-expert scatter/gather. These stages produce tail latency variance because they serialize per-token routing decisions and create bursty memcpy patterns.

Detailed observations and traces:
- Dense-L (Llama-like) at seq=8192, batch=1:
  - Per-layer breakdown: attention forward/back + kv-evict dominate (70% of token latency).
  - NVTX trace: repeated small kernels (~200us) for KV scatter; kernel-launch overhead accumulates (~30ms per 1k tokens).
  - Memory pattern: dense KV buffers allocated per-layer cause peak memory > expected theoretical. Short-term mitigation: reuse layer-specific KV buffers across layers where shape is identical.

- Dense-M (Mistral-like) at seq=8192, batch=8:
  - Chunked attention reduced FLOPs by ~20% vs Dense-L but increased kernel count by ~55% (more small ops).
  - Scheduler queuing: head-of-line blocking seen on the compute queue; smaller kernels increase overhead and reduce GPU SM occupancy. Observed 15–25% lower throughput than expected scaling.
  - Mitigation: fuse the chunked-attention elementwise steps into a single CUDA kernel across chunks (prototype suggests 18% wall reduction).

- Dense-Q (Qwen-like) at seq=8192, mixed batch:
  - Rotary positional embeddings well integrated — fewer reshapes and less scatter. Decode latency per token ~10–12% lower than Dense-L in single-session tests.
  - However, under concurrent workload with prefix caching, memory allocator fragmentation spikes. Cumulative fragmentation leads to failed allocations at ~92% of theoretical mem. Observed pattern: numerous short-lived allocations for attention indices + allocator free latency.
  - Mitigation: switch to a pooled allocator for index/temporary buffers and pre-reserve slab for expected max seq length.

- MoE routing synthetic (8-expert) at seq=4096, batch=4:
  - Router CPU path vs GPU: current router softmax + topk is on GPU but uses many small kernels. Topk argpartition is expensive for large token sets and produces variable fanout per-expert.
  - Hotspot trace: gating softmax kernel (~4–6ms per token), topk argpartition (~8–10ms), and per-expert scatter/memcpy (~10–25ms depending on expert size). End-to-end routing can be >40ms for single token in worst-case.
  - Observed contention: multiple threads attempt to schedule memcpy to the same expert buffer leading to serialization at CUDA stream boundaries.
  - Mitigations tested: a) batched routing decisions: accumulate routing for N tokens and process in one batched topk pass (reduces topk overhead by ~3x for N>=16), b) prefetch expert weights into tensor cores for predicted hot experts, c) per-expert submission queues to avoid stream contention.
  - Tradeoffs: batching increases latency for small tokens (adds jitter), prefetch requires memory headroom.

Micro-optimizations that moved metrics (ranked):
1) Small-kernel fusion (attention chunk elementwise ops) — consistent wins across Mistral-like workloads (~12–20% latency).
2) Pooled allocator for temporary buffers — reduced fragmentation OOMs and reduced free latency in Qwen tests (stabilized concurrent throughput by ~18%).
3) Batched routing for MoE topk — reduced the worst tail latency by up to 3x when batched; but worsened 50th percentile for micro-interactive workloads.
4) Per-expert submission queues — decreased writer contention and reduced memcpy serialization; complexity in backpressure handling introduced.

Profiling artifacts (how we collected):
- nvprof-like traces with per-kernel timestamps.
- Custom heatmaps: per-layer kernel time as matrix (layer x kernel-type) exported as CSV to GH issue linked above.
- Queue wait histograms (user-space): showed queue wait spikes aligning with routing bursts.

Recommendations / experiment backlog (next 6 weeks):
- Short term (quick wins):
  1) Implement pooled slab allocator for attention/index temporaries, enable by default for long-seq configs. (Owner: infra-alloc)
  2) Prototype fusion of chunked-attention ephemeral ops into a single kernel (Owner: serving-runtime, PR target: repo/serving-runtime#4321).
  3) Add per-expert submission queues guarded by lock-free ring buffers to minimize stream contention (Owner: routing-team).

- Medium term (2–6 weeks):
  1) Implement batched topk routing path with adaptive latency cap: dynamically choose batched vs immediate path based on current latency SLA/queue depth. (Owner: routing + sched)
  2) Expose allocator slab sizing knob in public config and add an initiate-warm path when loading long-context models. (Owner: runtime-config)

- Long term (quarter):
  1) Rework routing to produce sparse expert indices at construction time and leverage fused sparse kernels to apply expert ops without per-expert memcpy. Requires deeper kernel work and upstream lib changes.
  2) Evaluate multi-GPU pipelining for MoE expert execution with lightweight router shim on each device to reduce cross-device memcpy.

Open questions / experiments to prioritize for validation:
- How does fused-kernel performance scale on A10 vs A100 (smaller SM vs larger)? We saw different tradeoffs in occupancy; need a systematic sweep.
- Is there a golden slab size for pooled allocator that balances fragmentation and headroom across mixed workloads? We should run mixed-prod traces.
- For MoE: what is the cost of adding an LRU-prefetcher for experts? Can we detect “hot” experts robustly at runtime?

Appendix: quick commands used for reproducibility
- Run single-GPU trace:
  ./run_bench --model llama-13b --seq 8192 --batch 1 --trace nvtx --out traces/llama_8192.nvtx
- MoE batched topk experiment (local):
  ./run_moe --experts 8 --batching batched_topk --batch-size 16 --trace heatmap --out traces/moe_batched.csv

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Push heatmap exporter to GH issue and attach CSVs.
- Draft a micro-PR for pooled allocator and run canary on dedicated cluster.
- Sync with infra about allocator defaults for private deployments.

Conclusion:
Long-context behavior is a mix of compute and memory-allocation/launch overhead. Different architectures trade these costs differently: Mistral-style chunking lowers FLOPs but increases kernel overhead; Qwen layout reduces kernel scatter but stresses allocators; MoE adds routing fanout complexity that hurts tail latency. Practical gains are available via allocator improvements, kernel fusion, and adaptive batching for routing — each with tradeoffs for interactivity.
